newsitem.title: UK: Gerry Adams-the man N.I. unionists love to hate.
newsitem.headline: Gerry Adams-the man N.I. unionists love to hate.

text.p: Gerry Adams, once sought by the British army as a guerrilla suspect, has led his Sinn Fein party out of international isolation into a key role in Northern Ireland peace efforts.
Meanwhile the region's Protestant politicians have watched in horror as Adams has climbed from obscurity to become the respected voice of militant Irish republicanism in Europe and the United States.
David Trimble, leader of the biggest pro-British Unionist party, has described the eloquent, bespectacled Adams as "nothing more than a mouthpiece for the IRA and its murder squads."

They fear that Adams, whose party is the Irish Republican Army's political arm, fits neatly into Britain's long term plan to surrender a troublesome and bloody little part of the United Kingdom to Ireland and its Roman Catholic majority.
The Unionists, whose clarion calls are "No surrender" and "Not an Inch", have refused all direct contact with Adams or Sinn Fein for years.
Their deep mistrust of Adams will not be allayed by this weekend's IRA ceasefire, which will win his party a seat at the table at Northern Ireland peace talks, from which it has so far been excluded.
"Sinn Fein has never stopped trying for peace," he told a news conference on Saturday in the Roman Catholic West Belfast heartland where he was once suspected by Britain of being an IRA commander.
An unrepentant republican who sees Britain as an occupying force in Northern Ireland, Adams says he is striving for an end to strife and the removal of all guns from Irish politics.
Adams has been the polished public face of what political analysts have come to call the strategy of "armalite in one hand, ballot box in the other."

He walks a political tightrope forging a path to all-party negotiations between IRA "hawks" who say only violence will chase Britain from Ireland and "doves" who say that negotiations are the route to a United Ireland.

Adams persuaded the IRA to call a historic truce two years ago, and blames Britain's refusal to give Sinn Fein a seat in talks for its collapse in February 1996. Supporters say he has brought a new political sophistication to their quest.

His Sinn Fein political party has emerged from international isolation and political obscurity to poll 17 percent of votes in Northern Ireland's elections and return Adams and his chief lieutenant, Martin McGuinness, to the British parliament.

The IRA, despite setbacks, has grown into a force that has lobbed mortars into the British Prime Minister's official residence and London's Heathrow airport. Its leaders stay in the shadows, while Adams and McGuinness take the limelight.

IRA gunmen murdered two Northern Ireland policemen last month in a daylight ambush staged at the very moment that the British government had reopened contacts with Sinn Fein to explain how it envisaged overcoming the hurdle of IRA arms surrender.
Britain broke off contact with Sinn Fein. Adams said the deaths were to be regretted and so was the ending of contact.
Tall, bearded and with a penchant for tweed jackets and heavy knitted jumpers, he looks more like a professor of law than a man who lived on the other side of it for many years.

Britain banned his voice from the airwaves for several years but failed to silence him. Associates say his weapons are a razor sharp political brain that matches the machinations of the "civil service mandarins" in London, and his pen.

Known to jot down notes for short stories and other writings while bodyguards drive him across Ireland, his autobiography, "Before The Dawn", is an Irish best-seller and he can be seen autographing copies at Sinn Fein functions.
The book contains a short story by Adams, giving a fictionalised account of an IRA sniper's emotions as he lies in wait before opening fire and killing a British soldier.

His family was steeped in revolutionary politics. His forebears were in groups that were forerunners to the IRA and his father was interned - held without trial - and so was Adams, on suspicion of being a senior IRA commander.
Adams grew up in a Belfast where Catholics say they were treated as second class, deprived of jobs, houses and electoral rights because they were regarded as anti-state.
A survivor of murder bids by pro-British Protestant extremists, he took part along with with senior IRA commanders in 1972 peace talks with the British which proved abortive.

He is married with one child, a son, and keeps both out of the spotlight which has shone on him since the British began searching West Belfast houses for him when Northern Ireland's "Troubles" erupted in the early 1970s.
